text: Lesson one showed a vector's coordinates only mean something relative to a chosen set of reference directions. This lesson makes that precise — which sets of vectors actually qualify as valid reference directions, and how to test one by hand.

The span of a set of vectors is everywhere you can reach using only addition and scalar multiplication — the span of [1,0] and [0,1] in R squared is all of R squared. A basis is a minimal spanning set: it spans the entire space and is linearly independent, so nothing in it is redundant. R squared's standard basis is [1,0] and [0,1]; C squared's computational basis — the one quantum computing actually uses — has exactly the same structure, with ket-zero and ket-one playing the same role.

For two vectors in R squared, there's a fast independence test: build a 2 by 2 matrix from them and check the determinant. Take u equals 1,2 and v equals 3,4 — the determinant is 1 times 4 minus 2 times 3, which is negative 2, nonzero, so the set is independent. Now take u equals 1,2 and v equals 2,4 — the determinant comes out to zero, because v is exactly 2 times u. Both vectors lie on the same line, so one of them is completely redundant.

Every quantum gate you'll study is a matrix that transforms one basis representation into another, and that's only meaningful if the basis you start from genuinely spans the space and wastes no information. A basis that's secretly dependent would break the one thing the whole theory depends on: that every qubit state decomposes uniquely into its basis coefficients.
Next lesson asks how big a vector actually is, and why quantum mechanics insists a valid state vector always has norm exactly one.
